documents.title: Memo page 3 — education coverage pitch, signed Martha Hamilton
documents.subject: Martha Hamilton proposing a shift from D.C. schools general-assignment coverage to a broader education beat
documents.notes: Final page ('memo/3') of a multi-page internal memo; only this page is in the batch. Typed page with manual strikethroughs, heavy photocopy show-through bands, and Martha Hamilton's handwritten signature over the typed name.

pages.transcript:
memo/3

* There's probably research that demonstrates the opposite, too. It's an intriguing question. (Maybe we could do a sidebar on the common middle class dream about failure -- the one where you walk into class on the day of the big test and realize you haven't been to class all year. School must breed a fine fear of failure into people.)

Any of these stories could be written well from a metropolitan [word struck through] perspective.

Before, I was a general assignments reporter covering the D.C. schools. We had the Education Bureau sitting off in a corner, and I was circumscribed by jurisdictional problems.[strikethrough] I liked what * I did, as far as it went, but it left me interested in doing more -- in covering education as we cover medicine and have sometimes covered housing and other issues.

If you're interested, let's talk about ways I might move in this direction.

[handwritten signature] Martha Hamilton

documents.title: Post Unit News No. 99 — 'Discrimination at The Post: Pay Gaps Widen'
documents.subject: Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild bulletin comparing reporter, salesperson, and T-5 Data Programmer pay by race and sex, 1986 vs 1987
documents.notes: Single printed page of the Guild's 'Post Unit News' newsletter, No. 99, dated October 22, 1987, headlined 'Discrimination at The Post — PAY GAPS WIDEN'. Page ends '-over-'; continuation not in this batch.

pages.transcript:
Post Unit News
[Newspaper Guild logo]
Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild
No. 99        Date October 22, 1987

Discrimination at The Post
                        PAY GAPS WIDEN

The patterns of pay discrimination that have contributed over the years to low morale and wide gaps in the amount Washington Post managers are willing to pay their employees not only persist, but have widened significantly since management imposed its version of the contract in August.

If you needed a reason to understand why this contract is inadequate, here it is.

Last we looked, white males topped the salary scales in the best-paying jobs in many of the largest job categories at the Post. The news is this: despite the company's stated commitments to the hiring and nurturing of women and minorities, the practice of paying inequitably based on race and sex has not only continued--it's gotten worse.

For reporters--the largest single job category covered by the contract--the average salary for white males was $988.68 at the beginning of 1986. By September of 1987, that figure had jumped to $1,140.52.

Such a salary improvement is not the source of our complaints, however. The problem is that while white males were continuing to improve, females and blacks continued the slide away from parity.

The numbers compiled after the so-called impasse was declared in mid-August tell the story.

Across all classifications, white males average $332 more a week than black females, $204.39 more than white females and $230.66 more than black males.

Among reporters, the figures are reversed slightly, but the discrepancies remain just as stark. White male reporters, on the average, make $240.59 more a week than black females, a gap that is $43.24 wider than in January of 1986.

The gap has also grown by about $2 a week between white male and white female reporters and by about $15 a week between white male and black male reporters.

Among outside advertising salespersons, the gap also increased significantly. White males, on average, earned about $25 more a week than black males and black females in 1986, a disparity which has now increased to $96 weekly. White females in this classification earn on average $61.51 less than their male counterparts, up from a $43.03 average weekly difference in 1986.

And the gap among white men and white women who work as T-5 Data Programmers has opened dramatically, moving from an $8.33 average weekly difference in 1986 to an $86.07 average difference now.

There have been some improvements. Black females who are classified as managers, assistant managers, editors, deputy and associate editors have closed a more than $200 gap between their average salaries and salaries for white males.

But overall, the Post's record on equal pay for equal work sends a clear message to the rank and file at the Washington Post about which employees are valued at this company, and which are not.

These comparisons tell the story:

Reporters                          1/86        9/87

White males                       $988.68     $1,140.52
Black males                        920.46      1,057.39
White females                      859.37      1,008.56
Black females                      791.33     $  899.33

-over-

Affiliated with American Federation of Labor—Congress of [Industrial Organizations — footer cut off]

documents.subject: Side-by-side salary comparisons of Hamilton and Mayer against comparator reporters (a Brown who left in 1985, Warren Brown, Mills, John Mintz), with experience, starting salary, salary history, and explanation sections
documents.notes: Two pages bearing the header 'CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES — PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES'; clearly part of the same comparative-salary exhibit. Page order here is a best guess (Brown sections likely precede Mills/Mintz); both pages are mid-document continuations.

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Experience and Education
Brown started at the Post in the late 1970s as a reporter in Financial News. The Post is unable to provide information about his prior experience and education. Brown left The Post in 1985.

Starting Salary
The Post could not locate information about Brown's prior salary. Brown's starting salary was less than the salary of Hamilton at that time.

Salary History
Brown received five merit increases during his time at The Post -- all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received merit increases in the following years: 1981, 1982, 1983 and 1984.

Warren Brown

Warren Brown was paid slightly less than Hamilton on the 1992 to 1995 salary snapshots. Brown and Hamilton were paid similarly on the 1996 to 1999 salary snapshots. Brown was paid more than Hamilton on the 2000 salary snapshot and substantially more than Hamilton on the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots.

Brown was paid similarly to Mayer on the 1995 and 1997 salary snapshots. Brown was paid slightly more than Mayer on the 1996 salary snapshot. Brown was paid slightly less than Mayer on the 1998 and 1999 salary snapshots. Brown was paid slightly more than Mayer on the 2000 salary snapshot. On the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots, Brown was paid substantially more than Mayer.

Brown was paid less than Skrzycki on the 1992 to 1999 salary snapshots. On the 2000 salary snapshot, they were compensated similarly. On the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots, Brown was paid substantially more.

Experience and Education
Brown came to The Post in the mid-1970s as a reporter in National News. Brown became a reporter in Financial News in 1982 where he remains today. Prior to starting at The Post, Brown worked as a reporter for the Philadelphia Inquirer for three years. He had also previously worked as a reporter for the New Orleans States-Item for approximately a year and served as the Associate Editor for JET Magazine. Brown is a graduate of Xavier University and has a Masters in Journalism from Columbia University. He also obtained a New York Times fellowship for post-graduate study in journalism.

Starting Salary

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Mills was paid less than Mayer on the 1995 snapshot, slightly less than Mayer on the 1996 snapshot and more than Mayer on the 1997 and 1998 snapshots.

Experience and Education
Mills came to The Post in the mid-1990s as a reporter in Financial News. Prior to starting at The Post, Mills worked as a reporter for The Congressional Quarterly for approximately six and-a-half years. He also served as a reporter and Associate Editor for Photo Marketing Magazine for two and-a-half years and worked as an intern reporter for The Los Angeles Times for six months. Mills is a graduate of Michigan State University and has a Masters in Public Affairs from American University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Mills received approximately a 36 percent increase over his prior salary at the Congressional Quarterly. His starting salary was less than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

Salary History
Mills received eight merit increases during his time at The Post -- all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these merit increases in the following years: 1995, 1996, 1997 and 1998. He also received an approximate 10 percent salary increase from The Post in 1997 in response to an offer from a competing newspaper.

Explanation:
Mills covered telecommunications -- considered a highly valued and challenging position by The Post.

Mills was a highly valued reporter in the marketplace, receiving interest from other papers and publications -- evidenced by his later acceptance of a competing job offer in 1999. As a result, Mills was put on the fast-track, which increased his salary. Mills also received an approximate 10 percent salary increase from The Post in 1997 in response to an offer from a competing newspaper.

John Mintz

John Mintz was paid similarly to Hamilton on the 1992 to 1996 salary snapshots, except he was paid slightly more on the 1994 salary snapshot.

Mintz was paid similarly to Mayer on the 1995 salary snapshot and slightly more than Mayer on the 1996 salary snapshot (Mayer did not appear on the 1992 to 1994 salary snapshots).
